steps.title: Energy balance for a control volume
steps.why: Energy conservation for a fixed control volume at constant pressure (A2) says the enthalpy stored changes only by conduction and by the enthalpy that moving vapor and air carry across the boundary. The divergence theorem turns this into a local statement.
steps.operation: conservation of enthalpy in a fixed volume, divergence theorem
steps.latex: \partial_t H + \nabla\cdot\left(\mathbf{q} + h_v\mathbf{j}_v + h_a\mathbf{j}_a\right) = 0,\quad H = \phi\rho_i h_i(T) + (1-\phi)\left(\rho_a h_a(T) + \rho_v h_v(T)\right),\quad \mathbf{q} = -k(\phi,T)\nabla T

check.printed: every term converts to W m^-3

steps.title: Water mass balance
steps.why: Mass conservation for the water substance: the ice lost per unit volume per unit time, $-\rho_i\partial_t\phi$, becomes vapor, which is stored in the gas or carried away by $\mathbf{j}_v$. This identity is what makes the latent heat appear.

check.printed: used as a substitution inside check_s4

steps.title: Air mass balance
steps.why: Air is neither made nor destroyed. When ice grows, it pushes air out of the volume, and that air carries its enthalpy with it.

steps.why: The term $(c_v\mathbf{j}_v + c_a\mathbf{j}_a)\cdot\nabla T$ compared with conduction is a Péclet number $|\mathbf{j}|c\ell/k \sim 10^{-7}\cdot 1850\cdot 10^{-4}/0.02 \sim 10^{-6}$ for pore size $\ell \sim 100\,\mu$m, so it is dropped (A5).

steps.why: Write the divergence of the flux in components to get the residual R that is returned. Sublimation ($\partial_t\phi<0$) acts as a heat sink and deposition as a heat source.

assumptions_used: A1: $\phi(x,y,z,t)$ is a known, smooth field (given). A point is a mixture: ice with volume fraction $\phi$ and gas with volume fraction $1-\phi$, and both have the same local temperature $T$ (local thermal equilibrium across the diffuse interface).
A2: The pressure is nearly uniform and steady, so enthalpy is the conserved energy density. Pressure work $\partial_t p$, kinetic energy and viscous dissipation are neglected.

A3: The ice density $\rho_i$ is constant (ice is incompressible, and its thermal expansion is neglected). Because of this, the ice mass per unit volume is $\rho_i\phi$ and the latent term is $\rho_i L\,\partial_t\phi$. All other properties may depend on $\phi$ and $T$; the specific enthalpies depend only on $T$.
A4: Heat conduction obeys Fourier's law with an effective conductivity $k(\phi,T)$. The gas is a mixture of air and water vapor, and the energy each species carries is its enthalpy flux.
A5: Sensible heat that moving vapor and air carry, $(c_v\mathbf{j}_v + c_a\mathbf{j}_a)\cdot\nabla T$, is negligible compared with conduction (Péclet number about $10^{-6}$).

neglected.effect: Advection of sensible heat by vapor and air fluxes
Pressure work and changes in total pressure
neglected.why: Total pressure in the pore is nearly constant on the time scales of sublimation. $\partial_t p$ is many orders of magnitude smaller than $C\,\partial_t T$.

neglected.effect: Kinetic energy and viscous dissipation of the gas
neglected.why: Gas speeds are tiny (mm/s or less), so $\rho u^2/2$ is negligible next to the enthalpies (about $10^6$ J/kg).
The expansion coefficient is about $10^{-4}$ K$^{-1}$, so the extra terms are of relative order $10^{-4}\,\Delta T$.

neglected.effect: Interfacial (surface) energy and curvature (Gibbs-Thomson) correction to the latent heat
neglected.why: $\gamma/(\rho_i L\,r) \approx 0.1/(920\cdot2.8\times10^6\cdot10^{-6}) \approx 4\times10^{-5}$ for curvature radius $r \approx 1\,\mu$m. The phase-field equation for $\phi$ is a later task.

Effective radiative conductivity $4\sigma T^3\ell \approx 4\cdot5.7\times10^{-8}\cdot8\times10^6\cdot10^{-4} \approx 2\times10^{-4}$ W/(m K), small next to the conductivity of ice (about 2-4 W/(m K)). It matters only in nearly empty, large pores.
These cross effects are second order in dilute vapor diffusion.

neglected.effect: Heat exchange with the regolith grains
neglected.why: The task restricts the domain to the pore space. The grains enter only through boundary conditions.
